0739e9bce0d3: Why do the young Cratchits tell Martha to hide when their father arrives?
They want to play a happy trick and surprise him
They think he will be angry she came late
They want to keep her away from Tiny Tim
They are ashamed of her work clothes
The children are excited, “everywhere at once,” and cry “Hide, Martha, hide!” as a playful surprise for “father coming.”
What does the description of Bob’s clothes suggest about the Cratchit family?
They are poor but take pride in looking their best
They are wealthy and dress in fashion
They do not care how they look
They have bought new clothes for Christmas
His clothes are “threadbare” yet “darned up and brushed, to look seasonable,” showing poverty along with care and pride.
What is the effect of the narrator’s words “Alas for Tiny Tim”?
They make the reader feel pity for the sick child
They make Tiny Tim seem funny
They show the narrator dislikes Tiny Tim
They suggest Tiny Tim is about to get better
“Alas” expresses sorrow, and the detail that “he bore a little crutch, and had his limbs supported by an iron frame” invites sympathy.
e2a20a5db392: What is the narrator’s main feeling as he watches the two reptiles?
Awe and amazement at seeing ancient creatures alive
Boredom because he has seen them before
Anger at Hans for being right
He exclaims, “At last have mortal eyes gazed upon two reptiles of the great primitive ocean!” showing wonder.
In this passage, the word “prodigious” (describing the tail) most nearly means
The narrator is judging the creature’s size: “This one measures not less than a hundred feet in length,” and he sees it “lift his prodigious tail.”
How does the narrator help readers imagine the Ichthyosaurus?
He compares its parts to familiar things and gives exact measurements
He describes only its sounds and smell
He compares it to a tiny fish
He refuses to describe it because it is too frightening
He says its eyes are “as big, or bigger than a man’s head” and that it is “not less than a hundred feet in length.”
96f88c888354: What does the boy’s state of mind seem to be as he walks down the corridor?
Upset and fearful, feeling watched and judged
Joyful and relaxed after a good day
Bored and indifferent to his surroundings
Proud and eager to show off
His eyes are “weak and tired with tears,” and he imagines great men “looking down on him silently as he passed.”
Why is it significant that the boy only “thought” the shapes were portraits?
His imagination fills the dark with figures of authority
He can clearly see every painting in detail
He has been told exactly which paintings hang there
He is pretending not to see the paintings
It was so dark “he could not see. But he thought they were the portraits of the saints and great men of the order,” so the images come from his mind.
How does the long list of saints and great men affect the mood of the passage?
It builds a sense of the weight of tradition pressing on a small boy
It lightens the mood with humour
It suggests the boy is bored by history
It shows the corridor is bright and cheerful
The sentence piles up figures from “saint Ignatius Loyola” to “Father Peter Kenny sitting in a chair wrapped in a big cloak,” all silently overseeing him.
91ebaa4d5370: What does the description of Carton leaning “where its shadow was darkest” suggest about him?
He is an outsider who stays unnoticed and apart
He is the most popular man in the group
He is hiding because he committed a crime
He is waiting to arrest Mr. Darnay
He “had not joined the group, or interchanged a word with any one of them” and stood “where its shadow was darkest.”
What is ironic about the situation described in the passage?
Carton helped in the day’s events but no one gave him credit
Carton was praised by everyone in court
Mr. Stryver did all the work and was ignored
“Nobody had made any acknowledgment of Mr. Carton’s part in the day’s proceedings; nobody had known of it.”
What tone does Carton use when he speaks to Mr. Lorry and Mr. Darnay?
He teases, “Men of business may speak to Mr. Darnay now?” and jokes about “a conflict… in the business mind.”
212c5058ec90: Why does the Hatter turn pale and fidget?
He feels scared when the Queen stares at him
He is cold in the courtroom
He is excited to sell his hats
He has forgotten his own name
“the Queen put on her spectacles, and began staring at the Hatter, who turned pale and fidgeted.”
What is funny about the King’s words to the Hatter?
He tells him not to be nervous while threatening him
He thanks the Hatter for his hats
He speaks very kindly and softly
He forgets what he wanted to say
The King says “don’t be nervous, or I’ll have you executed on the spot,” which would make anyone more nervous.
Why does the Hatter say the hats are not stolen?
He keeps them to sell and owns none himself
He found them on the road
The Queen gave them to him
He made them for the King
He explains, “I keep them to sell… I’ve none of my own. I’m a hatter.”
e41df2762847: How does Alice feel when the Duchess says “You don’t know much”?
“Alice did not at all like the tone of this remark,” so she tries to change the subject.
What does Alice decide to do after the rude remark?
Help the cook with the soup
She “thought it would be as well to introduce some other subject of conversation.”
What is strange about how the Duchess acts when things hit her?
She does not seem to notice at all
“The Duchess took no notice of them even when they hit her,” which makes the scene silly and odd.
3b983c871b2a: What is the inner conflict that Alexey Alexandrovitch tries to suppress?
He secretly hopes his wife’s death will solve his problems
He fears he has caught her illness
He wants to stay in Petersburg forever
He doubts the train will arrive on time
He “could not drive away the reflection that her death would at once remove all the difficulty of his position,” something he “dared not hope for, and yet was hoping for.”
What does his two-part resolution reveal about his character?
He relies on rigid rules of propriety to control his feelings
He acts spontaneously from strong emotion
He is eager to forgive without conditions
He cares nothing for how things appear
His plan reads: “If it’s a trick, then calm contempt and departure. If truth, do what is proper.”
What purpose does the list of “Bakers, closed shops, night-cabmen, porters” serve?
It shows him fixing on surface details to avoid his own thoughts
It shows Petersburg is crowded and lively
It explains why he is late
It proves he loves the city
These things “flashed past his eyes, and he watched it all, trying to smother the thought of what was awaiting him.”
bb41aaacb1b0: What can you infer about Martha from Miss Sarah’s description?
She is stubborn and hates to throw anything away
She is easygoing and agrees with everyone
Martha kept the duckhouse “for fear it might come in handy sometime,” and “you might as well argue with a post as with Martha.”
What does the narrator suggest about Anne by saying she “was never meant to match business wits with a Copp”?
She is not a shrewd bargainer
She is cleverer than Miss Sarah
Anne offered twenty dollars right away, and the narrator says otherwise “she would not have offered her price at the start.”
The phrase “argue with a post” is an example of
a comparison showing how stubborn Martha is
a description of a real fence post
a sign that Martha cannot speak
a hint that Sarah enjoys arguing
Miss Sarah says “you might as well argue with a post as with Martha,” meaning Martha will not change her mind.
2edb32b52ba3: Why are the words “by the greatest chance in the world” placed in quotation marks?
To hint that the meeting was not really chance at all
To show the meeting was truly accidental
Because they are the title of a book
The narrator adds that the detective “was determined not to lose sight of him,” so the “chance” meeting was planned.
What is Fix’s real reason for wanting to walk with Mr. Fogg?
He wants to keep watching him
He wants to show him the city
He is lonely and wants a friend
The narrator explains that “the detective—who was determined not to lose sight of him—begged permission to accompany them.”
How does the author show the size of the crowd in Montgomery Street?
By listing every place, even roofs, filled with people
By giving the exact number of people
By describing a single quiet person
By saying the street was empty
“the side-walks, street, horsecar rails, the shop-doors, the windows of the houses, and even the roofs, were full of people.”
4e1d056369c4: What does the simile comparing Jane to a hunter show about her?
She leaps eagerly into a topic she loves discussing
She is tired and slow to answer
She is secretly a skilled rider
She bounds into the topic “with the exuberant plunge of a hunter when it leaves the high road and feels turf under its hoofs.”
What does naming the cocktail “an Ella Wheeler Wilcox” suggest about Clovis?
He has a mischievous, irreverent sense of humour
The narrator says he had “irreverently patented” the name for his drink.
In this passage, “paragon” most nearly means
Jane says Clovis’s mother is “so wonderfully lucky in her servants” and calls Sturridge “a paragon as butlers go.”
2069be349853: What do we learn about Alfred from what the horse tells us?
He lies about exercising the horse
He works the horse too hard
He is the horse’s kind master
He is an expert horse doctor
Alfred claims he noticed it “when I have exercised him,” but the horse says “he hardly ever did exercise me.”
Why does the horse feel ill and restless?
He is fed a lot but never gets exercise
He is given too little food
He sleeps outside in the cold
He stood “for days together without stretching my legs at all, and yet being fed just as high as if I were at hard work.”
The horse says Alfred was “as ignorant as he was conceited.” What does conceited mean here?
Alfred acts as if he knows best but gives the wrong care, being “altogether as ignorant as he was conceited.”
f220f3468c1f: What is the central change Thoreau describes after leaving prison?
He sees his neighbours and the State more clearly and critically
The town has physically aged and decayed
He has become more trusting of his community
He has decided to obey all laws
No great physical change occurred, yet “I saw yet more distinctly the State in which I lived” and “to what extent the people… could be trusted.”
What does Thoreau mean by saying his neighbours’ friendship was “for summer weather only”?
Their loyalty lasts only when it costs them nothing
They are only friendly during the summer months
He adds that “in their sacrifices to humanity they ran no risks, not even to their property.”
How does Thoreau soften his criticism at the end of the passage?
He admits he may be harsh and suggests they are unaware
He apologizes and takes back every claim
He praises the jail as a fine institution
He says the tax was fair after all
He writes, “This may be to judge my neighbors harshly; for I believe that most of them are not aware that they have such an institution as the jail.”
8822a0bb4dde: What does Raskolnikov’s obedience to Porfiry’s command reveal?
Porfiry has psychological power over him, which enrages him
He realises “with hatred that he could not help obeying the command and driven to even greater fury by the thought.”
How does Porfiry change briefly in this passage?
He drops his playful mask and becomes stern
He becomes more joking and gentle
He loses “the look of old womanish good nature” and is “peremptory, stern, frowning and for once laying aside all mystification.”
Raskolnikov whispers “though he was in a perfect paroxysm of fury,” after falling “into actual frenzy.”
33501a280a2e: Why does the narrator explain that faces often soften after death?
To quickly ease a painful doubt in the grieving man’s mind
To show off his medical training
To persuade him to leave the room
He says “such a horrible doubt should not have life for a moment longer than I could help,” and the explanation “seemed to quite do away with any doubt.”
What does the man’s farewell reveal about his feelings?
Deep, tender love and reluctance to leave her
Relief that the ordeal is over
Suspicion and fear of the body
He kisses her hand and forehead and leaves “fondly looking back over his shoulder at her as he came.”
What is the overall tone of the passage?
The narrator speaks “sadly,” and the man looks at her “lovingly and long” before saying good-bye.
fc45ad1282bb: What does the captain realise by the end of the passage?
The mate was the one who killed the missing crew
The ship is close to port
The mate survived in the sea
The fog was causing the madness
He concludes, “It was this madman who had got rid of the men one by one, and now he has followed them himself.”
How does the mate’s mood change just before he jumps?
From wild terror to calm despair
He arrives “a raging madman,” but then “His horror turned to despair, and in a steady voice he said.”
What is the effect of the repeated phrase “When I get to port!”?
It shows the captain doubting he will survive
It shows his confidence about arriving soon
It is an order to his crew
He repeats the phrase and then asks, “Will that ever be?” revealing fear and hopelessness.
b4b1e335e74f: Why does Emma’s colour rise at the start of the passage?
She is embarrassed by praise she feels she does not deserve
She is angry at Mr. Knightley
She is proud of her achievements
“Emma’s colour was heightened by this unjust praise,” and she shakes her head while looking at Mr. Knightley.
What does the frequent use of dashes contribute to the passage?
It mirrors Emma’s excited, rushing, uncertain thoughts
It marks spoken dialogue between characters
It signals a change of setting
Thoughts tumble out: “He took her hand;—whether she had not herself made the first motion, she could not say—she might, perhaps, have rather offered it.”
slow to act; inclined to delay
Knightley’s mind “could neither be undecided nor dilatory,” pairing it with decisiveness and “alertness.”
3105eab88cfa: What is the main purpose of this passage?
To give editorial background on the essay and the Abbey fee
To tell a story about Lamb’s childhood
To argue that Westminster Abbey should close
It is a note explaining the essay’s source in the “London Magazine, October, 1823” and the history of the “two-shilling fee.”
What does Lamb’s admission that his “guardian angel” had been “absent” suggest?
He later regretted the anger in what he wrote
He believed angels wrote his essays
He was proud of every word
He admitted it “afterwards, when his anger against Southey had cooled.”
How does the editor use evidence about the fee?
By comparing several sources that show reform came slowly
By relying on a personal visit
The editor cites Reynolds, J.T. Smith and Dean Stanley, noting the reprint “suggests that the reform still tarried” and fees were “lowered in 1841.”
f48bed976439: What is Emerson’s central claim in this passage?
Great and simple spirits meet life with playful freedom, not heavy seriousness
People must take every task with deep seriousness
Sports are harmful to good health
Children should be kept from play
He says “The great will not condescend to take any thing seriously; all must be as gay as the song of a canary.”
Why does Emerson praise the Master’s reply to Juletta?
It shows defiant spirit in the face of power
It shows the Master fears being hanged
The Master answers, “’Tis in our powers, then, to be hanged, and scorn ye,” and Emerson calls these replies “sound and whole.”
What does the image of “little children frolicking together” suggest?
Beneath serious appearances, humanity at its best is playful and innocent
Humans are foolish and should grow up
Children are the only happy people
History is a solemn, joyless story
Though people “wear a stately and solemn garb of works,” in vision they would appear “like little children frolicking together.”
e26112c3cf9d: How is the black-and-gold clock like “a person talking a foreign language”?
It seems wrong but makes sense once you know its code
It is too loud to understand
It never tells the time at all
“The black-and-gold clock always struck wrong, but it was all right when you knew what it meant.”
Why does Anthea put her face in cold water?
So she will not want to get back into bed
Because she is late for school
The narrator calls it “a fairy charm that prevents your wanting to get back into bed again.”
What does the way Anthea folds her nightgown show about her?
She is in a terrible hurry
She folded it “by the seams from the hem,” which shows “the kind of well-brought-up little girl she was.”
11ef2c21e679: What attitude does the stranger show toward the group?
“There was an expression of contempt on his face,” and he looked at everybody “coldly and sarcastically.”
What point is the stranger making with his question?
A person must be presumed innocent until proved guilty
Mr. Wopsle should become a judge
He asks if they know “that the law of England supposes every man to be innocent, until he is proved—proved—to be guilty.”
Why does the group react “as if it were the murderer” when the stranger speaks?
His sudden, unexpected voice startles them
They recognise him as the murderer
He has been shouting for a long time
They had not noticed him until then: “Everybody started and looked up, as if it were the murderer.”
51af8d6f48df: What is Gulliver’s attitude toward his fellow humans in this passage?
Contempt; he sees them as degraded Yahoos
Affection and pride in his family
Fear that they will punish him
He calls them “these miserable animals” and speaks of the “infernal habit of lying… so deeply rooted in the very souls of all my species.”
He scorns the idea that he must “defend my veracity,” claiming he cured himself of “lying, shuffling, deceiving.”
What is ironic about Gulliver’s complaint?
He claims superiority over humans while admitting his own Yahoo nature has revived
He praises Europeans as the most honest people
He says he never learned anything from his master
He insists he will keep reforming humans forever
He admits “some corruptions of my Yahoo nature have revived in me,” even while sneering at others.
215cf4195f64: Why does Clara drink the goat’s milk even though she hesitates at first?
She is very thirsty from the walk
She has always loved goat’s milk
She drank after “seeing how Heidi drank hers up without hesitating, and how much she seemed to like it.”
How does the grandfather feel when Clara finishes her milk?
He “had looked on with satisfaction at seeing her follow Heidi’s example.”
What does the grandfather believe the milk will do for Clara?
He says it “will make her strong” and offers, “To-morrow we will drink two.”
3c51febaa840: How does the news of the town’s fall affect Orwell’s view of the war?
It plants his first doubts about a war that had seemed morally simple
It convinces him the war is nearly won
It makes him trust the official reports more
It has no effect on his thinking
It “set up in my mind the first vague doubts about this war in which, hitherto, the rights and wrongs had seemed so beautifully simple.”
How does the passage show the way the truth reached the soldiers?
Gradually, moving from denial to rumour to official admission
All at once through a radio broadcast
It never reached them at all
They first “set it down as a lie,” then heard “more convincing rumours,” and it was later “admitted officially.”
What does the phrase “so beautifully simple” suggest about Orwell’s earlier outlook?
It was naive, and he now sees it with some irony
It was wise and he still holds it
It was confused from the start
It was based on careful study
By saying the rights and wrongs “had seemed so beautifully simple,” he looks back on his certainty after “the first talk I had heard of treachery or divided aims.”
48885ba53dc2: What is the main point Rochester is trying to make in this speech?
His love for Jane would endure even through sickness or madness
He wants Jane to leave him forever
He fears Jane is lying to him
He is angry that Jane misunderstood a joke
He insists, “Your mind is my treasure, and if it were broken, it would be my treasure still.”
What contrast does Rochester draw with “that woman”?
He would embrace Jane tenderly where he shrank from the other woman
He would treat both women exactly the same
He admires the other woman more
He would leave Jane with a nurse
He says, “I should not shrink from you with disgust as I did from her,” but “receive you in an embrace.”
What does Rochester’s sudden question “But why do I follow that train of ideas?” reveal?
He catches himself being carried away by emotion and turns to practical plans
He has forgotten what he was saying
He wants Jane to answer him
He is changing his mind about leaving
Right after the question he returns to business: “I was talking of removing you from Thornfield.”
b4cb2403ff65: Why can’t Leopard and the Ethiopian find Zebra and Giraffe?
Their stripes and blotches match the forest shadows
Zebra and Giraffe ran far away
It was too dark to see anything
Zebra and Giraffe were dug into holes
“all they could see were stripy shadows and blotched shadows in the forest, but never a sign of Zebra and Giraffe.”
What does the Ethiopian mean when he says Leopard is “like a bar of soap in a coal-scuttle”?
Leopard is easy to see in the dark forest
He says, “You show up in this dark place like a bar of soap in a coal-scuttle,” meaning Leopard stands out.
What lesson does the Ethiopian want Leopard to learn?
He calls hiding in the shadows “a trick worth learning” and says “Take a lesson by it, Leopard.”
290f9a711d0e: What feeling does Twain have as the boat sets out?
A comfortable sense that nothing has changed since his river days
Sadness at how different everything is
It was “as natural and familiar… as if there had been no break in my river life.”
Why does the cub make Twain nervous?
He leaves too much space between the boat and the ships
He steers too close to the ships
He refuses to take the wheel
“He made me nervous, for he allowed too much water to show between our boat and the ships.”
What is humorous about Twain’s final sentence?
He enjoys seeing someone else suffer the lesson he once suffered
He is upset the captain took the wheel
He wishes he were the cub again
He thinks the cub is a better pilot than he was
He takes “very great and sincere pleasure… to see the thing repeated—with somebody else as victim.”
40deb6bc630d: What is the main source of humour in this passage?
Two men compete to prove whose youth was harder and more innocent
Two men argue over who owns a box
A man is lost in a snowstorm
Robinson refuses to tell a story
One boasts of snow blowing in “a foot deep,” and Robinson replies, “you weren’t one-tenth as innocent as I was.”
Why is Robinson’s description of a “grand old life” ironic?
His example of wild living is only playing cards by candlelight
He describes dangerous adventures at sea
He admits he hated his childhood
He never actually speaks of his past
His proof of innocence is that “we’d sit round and play pedro by a candle half the night,” a very tame thrill.
What is Leacock satirizing in this passage?
People’s urge to exaggerate past hardships to look superior
Each man tries to top the other: “Not stand it!… I’m made for it,” even admitting “You’ll swear this is a darned lie.”
15e1009c848f: What does the line “Don’t laugh! Act as if it was all right!” suggest about the play?
Something has gone wrong and the actors are trying to carry on
The play is meant to be a comedy
The actors are rehearsing an ending
It comes after a mishap, since Roderigo was “decidedly shaken by the fall from the tower upon him.”
How does Hagar save the lovers?
She swaps the poisoned cups for harmless ones
She fights Hugo with a sword
She warns the servant not to deliver the wine
“Hagar changes the cups for two others which are harmless.”
What is the tone of the narrator’s description of the play?
Affectionately amused at the dramatic, homemade performance
Details like the retainer “evidently forgetting the speech he ought to have made” and Hugo’s “clutching and stamping” are gently comic.
0b3d6eb88997: What has the cold done to John Messner’s spirit?
It has made him dull and unobservant
It has made him excited and alert
It has made him angry at his dogs
It has made him want to turn back
“The frost was benumbing his spirit. He plodded on with bowed head, unobservant.”
What does the water-hole suggest to Messner?
Someone has lived nearby, though not recently
The river is about to flood
The dogs have dug it themselves
Wild animals use it every day
It was “chopped laboriously with an axe,” and “A thick skin of new ice showed that it had not been used for some time.”
What contrast does the author draw between the man and the dogs?
The dogs stay alert while the man has given in to apathy
The man is alert while the dogs are lazy
Both are equally exhausted and blind
The dogs are afraid while the man is calm
Messner was “succumbing to the apathy of it all,” but “the dogs were observant” and were “already pointing the way.”
ef1077563fe9: What do the details about crushing bones show about the man’s condition?
He is starving so badly that he barely notices pain
He is enjoying a hearty meal
He is preparing food for others
He pounds his fingers and feels “surprise at the fact that his fingers did not hurt much,” so desperate is his hunger.
What does the author mean by “It was the life in him, unwilling to die, that drove him on”?
A deep survival instinct, not his conscious will, keeps him moving
He has a clear plan to reach home
Another person is helping him travel
He wants to die but cannot
The narrator says “He, as a man, no longer strove,” so something deeper than his will drives him.
The image of life that “flickered up and burned less dimly” compares the man’s life to
a weak flame that might go out
He “crawled on whenever the dying life in him flickered up and burned less dimly,” like a fading fire.
52bbc7232dd5: What is the point of the frankincense image in section XII?
Every life ends sooner or later, and the order makes no real difference
Religious ritual is the key to happiness
Some people deserve to live longer
“one drops first and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.”
What does section XI urge the reader to do?
Actually use one’s reason, since it is enough
Doubt that one has reason at all
He asks, “Why then makest thou not use of it? For if thy reason do her part, what more canst thou require?”
What does section XIII suggest about other people’s opinions?
They are fickle and change quickly, so they should not guide us
They are always fair and wise
They should be earned at any cost
Those who now think you “a mere brute, and of an ape” may, “Within ten days,” esteem you “a god.”
58dfe25598ce: What is the tone of Melville’s comparison of the King’s law to “halving an apple”?
Dryly humorous, pointing out the absurd neatness of the division
Splitting a whale into head and tail is “much like halving an apple; there is no intermediate remainder,” a wry observation.
Why does Melville compare the separate chapter to a railway car for royalty?
To mock the special privilege given to royalty
To show he admires English railways
To explain how whales are transported
To suggest the chapter is very long
He treats it separately “on the same courteous principle that prompts the English railways to be at the expense of a separate car, specially reserved for the accommodation of royalty.”
an odd exception to the rule
The law “offers in various respects a strange anomaly touching the general law of Fast and Loose-Fish.”
6587dd93ae52: Why was the Mono Trail built?
A rush to newly discovered gold mines made it necessary
To bring tourists to the lake
For sheep to reach summer grass
The mines “were reported to be rich when first discovered, and a grand rush took place, making a trail necessary.”
What does the passage suggest about how much work went into the trail?
Very little; most of the land was left as it was
Huge amounts; it was fully paved
It took decades of careful engineering
Apart from a few bridges and lanes, “over the greater part of the way scarce a stone or shovelful of earth has been moved.”
crossing a stream by walking through it
Bridges were built “where fording was not practicable on account of the softness of the bottom.”
37cf26751093: What is Russell’s central position on mysticism?
It is valuable as an attitude toward life but mistaken as a belief about the world
It is entirely false and harmful
It is the only path to scientific truth
He writes, “mysticism is to be commended as an attitude towards life, not as a creed about the world.”
How does Russell connect science and mysticism?
Science may be nourished by the same spirit of reverence
Science and mysticism can never share anything
Science, “the very antithesis of the mystic’s swift certainty, may be fostered and nourished by that very spirit of reverence.”
What does the phrase “by sufficient restraint” show about Russell’s approach?
He accepts part of mysticism only with careful limits
He wants people to give up all emotion
He believes mysticism needs no limits
He thinks restraint is a mystical idea
He says “while fully developed mysticism seems to me mistaken… by sufficient restraint, there is an element of wisdom to be learned.”
b0efa42ceb95: According to Douglass, why was the master so cruel to Henny?
She was nearly helpless and seemed a useless expense to him
She had tried to run away
She had stolen from his store
“The secret of master’s cruelty toward “Henny” is found in the fact of her being almost helpless… She was to master a bill of expense.”
What device does Douglass use when he calls his master “benevolent”?
Irony, meaning the opposite of what he says
A simile comparing him to an animal
The “benevolent” master “set her adrift to take care of herself” — to “starve and die!”
What hypocrisy does Douglass expose in the last sentences?
A religious man claims to care for slaves while abandoning a helpless one
A poor man pretends to be rich
A slave pretends to be free
A doctor refuses to treat patients
He was “a recently-converted man,” one of the “pious slaveholders who hold slaves for the very charitable purpose of taking care of them.”
32470314e2fd: Why can’t Johnny Chuck keep up with Peter Rabbit?
“Johnny Chuck couldn’t keep up though he tried very hard, for Johnny’s legs are short.”
Why does Peter come back “walking very softly” and whispering?
He does not want to scare off what he has found
He tiptoes back and whispers, “I’ve found something,” keeping quiet about his discovery.
What does the phrase “though he tried very hard” tell us about Johnny?
He does his best even when it is difficult
He does not care about Peter
Johnny “couldn’t keep up though he tried very hard,” so he keeps trying.
e04b25b5b344: What does Sikes’s back-and-forth wandering reveal about his state of mind?
He is restless and cannot settle because of guilt and fear
He is enjoying a peaceful country walk
He is searching for a lost friend
He knows exactly where he is going
He goes “back towards London… then back again… and starting up to make for some other spot, and do the same.”
Why does he leave Hendon without buying food?

“the very children at the doors—seemed to view him with suspicion,” and he turned back “without the courage to purchase bit or drop.”

af1b20974478: What does Darwin argue is missing from simply concluding that species descended from other species?
